items.title: Wendell Brunious interviewed by Monk Rowe, Scottsdale, Arizona, April 16, 2000 [interview 2 of 2]
items.q: And then he worked and wrote for Billy Eckstine.

ctx.x: Oh gee, I didn’t know that.

And I used to say that to Diz sometimes, and Diz would say, “Man, I went on to be famous, I’m glad — they could take that job man.” So just imagine. And then he worked and wrote for Billy Eckstine. And when he was 28 years old he was ranked as the 6th

trumpet player in the Down Beat poll. And he got arthritis in his legs and he couldn’t walk for two years. And I mean if you have three kids at home and you can’t walk for two years, you know, I mean writing arrangements — I don’t know what arrangements paid back in the 40s some time, but it just, you know like decimated his whole economic situation. So he never really got back from that. He did pretty well but he never got to that step. I mean he died of a broken heart. He just always wanted to get back there.…

items.title: Wendell Brunious interviewed by Michael Woods, Los Angeles, California, September 3, 1995 [interview 1 of 2]
items.q: he played with Cab Calloway, the Billy Eckstine band, the Walter Fats Pichon band

ctx.x: Talk to us about, I caught a couple of your sets, which were just beautiful. Talk to us about your tone and some of your influences on the trumpet. You’ve already talked about Louis. But who did you listen to to help you formulate your tone and the way you play? Because the way you play is quite distinctive.

Yes, well thank you. It’s — my dad was a trumpet player, a really great trumpet player. He went to Juilliard Conservatory and he played in the, like I said earlier, he played with Cab Calloway, the Billy Eckstine band, the Walter Fats Pichon band, which is a band few people have heard of but that was a killer band. They played on the S.S. Dixie. They went up and down the Mississippi River. Man, Fats Pichon was a great writer, and he taught my dad a lot after my dad got out of Juilliard. I mean you know you learn…

Holiday and all of that stuff. So I grew up listening to really good music. I mean quite naturally, in the late ‘60s and early 70s when I started, I was a little teenager and I started first playing, and I played in all these rock bands you know. We were trying to play like Chicago and Blood Sweat and Tears type of stuff, which I thought was very well constructed music, still. But I had heard all of these Louis Armstrong doing like “I’m in the Market for You” with all of these beautiful, high notes, just coming…
